overview:
Out of the collapse of the Russian Empire in 1917 came a state that at first had no settled name. The Bolsheviks took power in Petrograd in November, and the Third All-Russian Congress of Soviets formally proclaimed a Russian Soviet Republic in January 1918; a constitution followed that July, giving the new order a federal shape meant to accommodate the many nationalities living across the old imperial space. That federal principle produced a nested hierarchy of autonomous republics, autonomous oblasts and okrugs, krais and ordinary provinces that would survive, with adjustments, for the next seven decades. When the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics was created by treaty in December 1922, the Russian republic was one of four founding signatories — and by far the largest, holding roughly three quarters of the union's territory and more than half its people, with the union capital, Moscow, sitting inside it.

That dominance came with a strange institutional emptiness. Precisely because Russia was the core, it was denied much of the apparatus the smaller republics had: for most of Soviet history there was no separate Russian communist party, no distinct Russian academy of sciences, no full set of republican ministries to speak for Russian interests against the centre. All-Union institutions did that work, which meant that Russian identity and Soviet identity were deliberately blurred, and that the republic's borders were treated as administrative rather than national — the transfer of Crimea to the Ukrainian SSR in 1954 was, at the time, an internal reshuffle of little apparent consequence. Through the Stalin years the republic was industrialised at enormous human cost, and by the postwar decades its oil, gas, metals and heavy industry underwrote the whole union economy; by the late 1970s that economy had slowed into stagnation, and Gorbachev's reforms of the late 1980s loosened political control faster than they fixed anything.

The institutional gap then turned into a weapon. On 12 June 1990 the Russian republic's Congress of People's Deputies declared state sovereignty, asserting that Russian law outranked all-Union law on Russian soil — a move that created something close to the dual power of 1917, with Gorbachev speaking for the union and Boris Yeltsin, popularly elected Russian president in June 1991, speaking for its largest part. After the failed August coup the centre had little left to defend. On 8 December 1991 Yeltsin met the Ukrainian and Belarusian leaders at Viskuli in the Belovezha Forest and signed accords declaring that the USSR had ceased to exist, replaced by a Commonwealth of Independent States; whether three republics could lawfully dissolve a union of fifteen was disputed then and is disputed still. Most of the remaining republics acceded at Alma-Ata on 21 December, and on 25 December, as Gorbachev resigned, the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic was renamed the Russian Federation.
significance: For most of the twentieth century this republic was the load-bearing centre of the world's largest state and of a global political project: the base from which the Soviet Union industrialised, absorbed the worst of the war against Nazi Germany, built a nuclear arsenal and sustained a superpower rivalry. Its internal design outlived it. The nested autonomies drawn up to manage imperial diversity became the map of the modern Russian Federation, and the ethno-territorial logic behind them supplied both the language of Tatar and Chechen claims in the 1990s and the borders that fifteen new countries inherited in 1991. That the union's dissolution was driven from Russia rather than only from the periphery — and settled by three men in a forest lodge — left a legal and emotional argument about legitimacy that has shaped Russian politics and its relations with its neighbours ever since.
coverage: Written from general reference works and a university teaching archive; the dataset itself holds no events beneath this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date. The narrative leans heavily on the beginning and the end — 1917–22 and 1990–91 are far better documented in accessible sources than the long middle, and the internal texture of the republic as distinct from the union (its own budget, its autonomous republics, its non-Russian peoples) is thin here. Soviet-era statistics on population, output and repression were shaped by the state that produced them, and casualty and famine figures for the 1930s remain genuinely contested.
